newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers, bosses set talks to end protests.
newsitem.headline: French truckers, bosses set talks to end protests.

text.p: French unions and haulage bosses set talks on Thursday as a four-day truckers protest blocking roads and fuel depots showed signs of squeezing the economy.

But Michel Caillaud, head of the National Federation of Truck Drivers (FNCR) said he was not certain the discussions, set for 1530 GMT, would address the unions' demands for wage hikes, retirement at 55 instead of 60 and shorter working hours.
"What they (employers) are ready to discuss does not necessarily correspond to our demands," Caillaud said.
The Communist-led CGT union said about 50,000 trucks were taking part in the protests and the drivers were bent on continuing their action until their demands were met.
"The ball is in their court. We'll continue to barricade the roads until clear points have been negotiated," said Jean-Pierre Prou of the General Workers' Confederation (CGT).
Car maker PSA Peugeot Citroen said that it had reduced shifts at several plants because of a shortage of spare parts, and some supermarkets and petrol stations were running low on supplies.

Motorways in and out of 30 towns and cities across the country were blocked by trucks, recalling a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a protest against a new points system for driving licences.
But Paris was spared after some disruption on Wednesday.

Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, whose mayor is Prime Minister Alain Juppe, as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight was badly hit.
Toulouse, Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Caen, Le Mans and the Franco-German border at Strasbourg were badly affected.
"This situation is dangerous and unacceptable," the Force Ouvriere (FO) union said in a statement. "(We) demand that negotiations start immediately on the basis of our demands."

In the southeast, truckers prevented access to fuel depots in Porte-les-Valence, Le Pontet and Bassens near Avignon, and a Shell refinery in Berre near Marseille, cutting supplies to service stations in the area.
Two of three fuel depots in the western Calvados department were blockaded and access to the port of Rouen was closed off.
Hundreds of police were deployed to keep roads open around the Mediterranean port of Marseille as dozens of trucks headed for the city, France's third largest.
Thousands of other trucks stood idle on parking lots across the country.
